newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:

AMLC COMMENTARY: Large supplies of cattle that have flooded saleyards over the past month have shown up in April Australian beef export volumes, the largest since November 1994.
Shipments rose to 72,906 tonnes, up 9,585 tonnes on March and 21 percent up on April 1996.
Exports to the U.S. were the largest since September 1994 at 25,231 tonnes. Canada, with 3,919 tonnes, and Taiwan, with 3,833 tonnes, also imported levels not reached since 1994.
Consignments to Japan and Korea were also higher than recent months, at 26,683 tonnes and 3,646 tonnes respectively.
Although tonnages increased, export beef prices were on the wane for most of April. Coupled with larger saleyard numbers, this led to a slide in prices.

However, the downward price trend abated this week as numbers offered tightened considerably. The dearth of good quality stock coupled with reduced numbers saw price rises of around four cents a kg liveweight for suitable cattle. Tighter overall supplies helped maintain prices for average and plain quality stock, despite these cattle being in the majority. The value of very plain quality stock fell again this week despite lower yardings.

Over the hook quotes were revised down by between five and 10 cents a kg dressed weight for most categories through the week, indicating the firm price trend in saleyards was more a reflection of lower supplies than a strengthening in end user demand.
Export beef values were quoted lower for most items in Australia's major markets.

In Japan, export prices fell by three to five U.S. cents a pound for most chilled items, equating to falls of between 14 and 24 Australian cents a kg. The market was quiet because of the Golden Week holiday and is likely to remain so as the holiday continues over next week. Although official figures have not been released, it seems that consumer buying for Golden Week was substantially below previous years.
Figures released by the Japanese Agriculture and Livestock Industry Corp for January and February show that Japanese beef consumption was down 7.4 percent on the same period in 1996.
Japanese domestic production fell by 10 percent over the same period.
Japanese import figures for March released this week show that March beef imports were nine percent below March 1996.

Although Australia's share rose to 55 percent, supplies from Australia were down by 5.5 percent over the month. Difficulties faced by exporters to the Japanese market are highlighted by the fact that total beef imports to Japan over the first quarter of 1997 are down by 13 percent.

In the U.S. this week, manufacturing beef prices also drifted lower, again pressured by larger domestic cow kills and competitive offers from New Zealand, which is in the middle of its annual cow slaughter. For the first time in months, beef on the U.S. spot market is trading at a discount to forward sales. Prices for Australian lean product fell by seven Australian cents a kg to 209 cents a kg FAS.

Solid demand in the U.S. over the spring-summer period will be imperative to soak up larger supplies of beef anticipated from U.S. feedlots soon. Slaughter levels are creeping toward 700,000 head a week, up around 30,000 head from March and early April levels. Carcase weights, however, remain lighter than a year ago, keeping production increases in check for the present.

The live cattle trade to the Middle East remains vibrant. Over the past month the trade has gained strength from reductions in European Union (EU) export subsidies on live cattle and beef exports. Australia's main competitors in this region are EU exporters.

Since the start of 1997, the European Commission has reduced subsidies by 10 percent in January and 7.5 percent in March. The latest cut, of five to 18 percent for live cattle and 18 percent for beef, came into effect from April 17.
The reductions are similar to those introduced around the same time last year and have been made to keep EU subsidised exports in line with GATT obligations.

For the year to March, Australian live cattle exports to Libya and Egypt totalled 21,750 head. However, in April alone shipments totalled 16,000 head, mostly to Egypt as the lower EU export subsidies lessened its competitiveness in these markets.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
